meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If you think you are too small to make a difference, try sleeping with a mosquito'?
meta.ogDescription: Disputed. First documented as a Body Shop lorry slogan in Time, 25 January 1993 — the Dalai Lama attribution only appears from 2004 onward.

answer.label: Not the Dalai Lama — a Body Shop slogan from the 1990s
answer.authorDates: 1942–2007 · British entrepreneur, founder of The Body Shop
answer.sourceLine: The earliest documented appearance of this saying is a January 1993 Time profile of Anita Roddick, where it is a slogan painted on the side of a Body Shop lorry — and even there Roddick is quoting her own truck, not claiming authorship. No speech, book, or interview of the 14th Dalai Lama has ever been produced for it; Wikiquote files it under Disputed and dates the first attribution to him to 2004.
answer.confidenceText: Disputed — the wording predates any Dalai Lama attribution by more than a decade, and no source establishes either of them as the author.

docMeta.dd: A slogan painted on the side of a Body Shop lorry

source.excerpt: IF YOU THINK YOU’RE TOO SMALL TO HAVE AN IMPACT, TRY GOING TO BED WITH A MOSQUITO
trail: January 1993 — the earliest known example. Wikiquote ↗ cites Philip Elmer-DeWitt’s Time profile of Anita Roddick, in which the line appears as a slogan taken from the side of a Body Shop lorry.
November 1995 — quote researcher Barry Popik’s next citation is an advertisement in an Ohio newspaper, the Bryan Times, reworking the line for a water-conditioning company. See his citation trail ↗.
Late 1990s onward — the saying is relabelled an “African proverb.” Popik notes the attribution is undocumented ↗ and reaches no conclusion about the true origin.
2004 — the first attribution to the Dalai Lama that Wikiquote can date ↗, which is why the entry sits under Disputed rather than among his sourced quotations.
source.excerptNote: The lorry slogan as capitalised in the 1993 Time profile and transcribed on Wikiquote ↗. Note the differences from the version now circulated under the Dalai Lama’s name: “have an impact” rather than “make a difference,” and “going to bed with” rather than “sleeping with.”
source.rightsNote: No author or first publication has been established for this wording, so no rights status can honestly be asserted — and certainly not public domain. The earliest text that carries it, the January 1993 Time article, is itself a modern in-copyright work; the slogan it reports has no identified author at all.

author.name: Anita Roddick
author.heading: About Anita Roddick
author.metaLine: 1942–2007 · British entrepreneur, founder of The Body Shop
author.bio: Dame Anita Roddick opened the first Body Shop in Brighton in 1976 and turned it into a global chain that campaigned on animal testing, human rights and environmental causes as loudly as it sold soap. She was famous for using her own delivery lorries as rolling billboards for slogans, which is how the mosquito line first reached print. She is the earliest name documented alongside the saying — but not, on the available evidence, provably its author.

misattribution.heading: Who it gets pinned on
misattribution.intro: This line has changed owners at least three times in thirty years, and each new owner made it sound older and wiser than the citation trail supports.

items.why: Wikiquote lists the saying in its Disputed section for the Dalai Lama and records the earliest attribution to him as dating from 2004 ↗ — more than a decade after the saying was already in print. No speech, teaching or book of his has been produced containing it.

Barry Popik notes the “African proverb” label attached to the saying without documentation, and Wikiquote points to a 2010 blog post using it; neither turns up a proverb collection or any pre-1993 source. Popik’s citation trail ↗ leaves the origin unresolved.

Roddick is the earliest name attached to the line, but Time presented it as a slogan she took from the side of one of her own company’s lorries — a favourite, not a coinage, as Wikiquote transcribes it ↗. Her own Wikiquote page ↗ does not carry the line at all.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer: nobody has traced an author. The trail runs back to a Body Shop delivery truck and stops, and the researcher who compiled the citations ↗ says so plainly.

context.heading: Why this one sticks to the Dalai Lama
lead: The saying is a perfect fit for a certain kind of inspirational feed: short, funny, faintly Buddhist in shape, and entirely unfalsifiable in a caption. The Dalai Lama is one of the internet’s most reliable magnets for that profile — a globally recognised name whose actual published output is large enough that nobody bothers to check whether a given line is in it.

What the paper trail actually shows is a commercial slogan. In January 1993 Time described Anita Roddick’s Body Shop lorries as rolling billboards for pithy lines, and printed this one in capitals. From there it drifted: an American water-treatment advertisement reworked it in 1995, it was relabelled an “African proverb” by the late 1990s, and only in 2004 did it start arriving with the Dalai Lama’s name on it.
detailsBody: Roddick’s own claim on it is weaker than the internet assumes too. Time presents the line as something she took off the side of one of her company’s lorries — a favourite slogan, not a coinage. Popik’s survey of the early citations ends with the origin unresolved, which is where an honest answer has to stop.
context.pull: A slogan on the side of a delivery truck became, in about a decade, the wisdom of a Nobel laureate.
